newsitem.title: USA: Citadel announces punishments in hazing scandal.
newsitem.headline: Citadel announces punishments in hazing scandal.

text.p: The Citadel said Monday it dismissed one male student and gave nine others lesser punishments after finding they had hazed two of the military college's first women cadets.

Maj. Gen. Clifton Poole, Citadel interim president, told a news conference one of the nine had been given the maximum punishment short of expulsion. He said one other cadet was cleared. The accused cadets were not identified by name.
"Hopefully, this will bring a conclusion to this most dark chapter in the Citadel's history," he said.

Boards appointed by the Citadel's commandant held closed hearings March 1 and 2 into the alleged involvement of 11 cadets in the hazing of Jeanie Mentavlos and Kim Messer, two of the first four women enrolled at the state-funded school after it dropped its all-male admissions policy last summer.

Shannon Faulkner, the first woman to join the corps of cadets after waging a more than two-year legal battle to change the Citadel's long-time all-male policy, dropped out during her first week at the school in August 1995.

Mentavlos and Messer, who did not return to the Citadel after their first semester ended in December, alleged physical abuse and sexual harassment by male cadets. Among other things, they said the clothing they were wearing was sprayed with fingernail polish remover and then set on fire.

Fifteen male cadets had faced a total of 36 charges in connection with the hazing. The Citadel said it had dealt with the most serious allegations in December, when two of the implicated cadets resigned rather than face charges and a third did not return for the second semester. A fourth was punished after appearing before a disciplinary board.

The cadet whose dismissal was announced Monday, a junior, had been accused of directing another cadet, in front of witnesses, to set Mentavlos' sweatshirt on fire. He then allegedly kicked the young woman to put the fire out.

The senior cadet given the maximum punishment short of expulsion will be restricted to campus until graduation, do 120 hour-long marches around the campus and be reduced in rank to private, officials said.

Poole said the school also had taken steps to ensure such improper activity would not take place again. He said he expected a report within two weeks from a committee developing plans for an easier transition to co-education.
"There is nothing further that we can do," Poole said. "We have investigated, we have charged and we have punished."

He noted that applications from women to the Citadel had risen, with 42 having applied for enrollment next fall. He said he hoped that at least 25 women would be included in the freshman class each year.

One of the other cadets whose punishment was announced Monday, a senior, had been accused of pushing the women and kicking them when they fell on the floor, requiring them to stay in a "pushup" position for a long time and forcing Messer to drink an entire pitcher of tea.

After the closed hearings, which Mentavlos and Messer did not attend, he was found guilty of gross poor judgment and violating the Citadel's "fourth class system," which governs the conduct of upperclassmen including forbidding them to touch first-year students. His punishment included mandatory sensitivity training, reduction in rank to private and restriction to campus until May 15.
Poole also said the U.S. Justice Department had attorneys on campus Monday doing interviews with cadets but the Citadel was not involved in that process.
The other cadets received punishments including mandatory sensitivity training, reduction in rank to private, forced marches and being confined to a seated position for a long period of time.
